fxyogi wrote: Hi HG,

If you don't mind, i would like to ask a question. I have taken the same trades you posted and drawn some zone with SD trader perspective. Please see the first image. A SD trader will mark yellow highlighted zone and short the move where you pointed out as fakie.

and the second image, the same trader would have taken demand became supply zone and short the move.

Hence,for me it looks like these two concepts are looking similar except the zone that we draw.

In WRB you mark the WRB hidden gap candle as a zone.SD trader will mark base as the zone. As an experience trader, you might have some logic behind using WRB HG method instead of Sam seiden's SD method.

Could you kindly shed some light on this.

The easy answer is that I found WRB Analysis first and after looking through that prism it's hard to change to Sam's SD method.

The harder, and truer, answer has to do with how and why I was attracted to WRB analysis in the first place. I came to WRB analysis after I started my journey into Volume Spread Analysis (VSA). Tom Williams would talk a lot about looking for a low volume narrow spread (range) interval within the spread(range) of a high volume interval. After looking at numerous charts, I was able to see the validity of his claim. Many good trade set-ups were indeed occurring in the range of a wide spread high volume interval. As I was seeing this phenomenon, I came across a post by Mark where he mentioned WRBs. While Mark did not use VSA, I immediately thought that there must be some connection. Or at the very least, they would be compatible. Despite the fact that Mark was originally dealing with the body of a candle and VSA does not look at the open, WRB (Wide Range Body) analysis proved to be very usable with VSA.

By the time I was introduced to Sam's work, I was already a firm believer in the power of the concept of a WRB hidden gap. I also have a problem with one aspect of Sam's method highlighted by your second picture. I do not believe that a Supply/Demand Zone is a trade signal in and of itself. Nor do I believe that Supply/Demand Zones can change polarity. Actually, I should say that in all the videos I have watched, Sam never mentions that zones can reverse polarity. Yet in all the threads I read about SD, the concept of supply becoming demand and vice versa is used.

I don't think this is accurate. If a demand zone is created by a rally base rally pattern and a supply zone is created by a drop base drop pattern, then the only way a demand zone can become a supply zone is if there is a drop base drop at the exact same place. In other words, merely cutting through a demand zone and then finding support (a totally different concept than supply and demand) does not in my opinion constitute a change in polarity. I like the fact that all zones close in WRB analysis. There is no concept of reversing polarity. Which is really a concept of support and resistance.

Hello my friend. The Fakie (or Fakey) is a price action pattern that comes from Nial Fuller's site. There are a few FREE videos on his site or youtube showing it with a bit more detail than follows.

Basically, the Fakie (or Fakey) is a price action pattern that requires there to be a false-break of an inside bar setup. So, once you have an inside bar setup, you can watch for a false-break of the inside bar and the mother bar.

Take a look at the chart below.

A. Is called the Mother candle. We only know it is the Mother candle after we see B. B. Inside interval. That means this interval does not make a higher high or a lower low than the previous candle. C. This interval makes a false break of the high of both the inside bar and the Mother candle, but it closes back within the range of the Mother candle.

Note that the intervals between X and Y also form a fakie. However, this would never be taken because no part of any interval in the pattern is occurring within a valid Supply/Demand Zone.

The false break must be on the first interval that trades outside the range of the Mother candle.

gristar wrote: Hi HG! good day to u. Other than fakie and engulfing, what is other entry signal you use? Do we enter whenever we see engulfing or fakie in hidden gap? We do not care if the entry signal happen at top or bottom part of the hidden gap if the hidden gap is very wide range? Can you show some example when a open hidden gap become closed zone. How aboutstop loss placement,is it at the end of fakie or end of delta zone? Hope to hear from you soon. Thanks in advance.

Hello Gristar.

Lots of questions there. Awesome!

I want to first focus on the issue of a zone closing. Take a look at the chart. There are three (3) possible ways a zone can be considered closed. That is to say, each individual can choose which method he or she prefers and then stick to that one for consistency.

Methods

#1. One can consider the zone closed, after price action has filled the zone.

#2. One can consider the zone closed, after price action closes above the zone (for a Supply Zone).

#3. One can consider the zone closed, after a full candle body (white for a Supply Zone) is formed above the the Zone. This body should not be a doji.

I prefer #3. If the interval in question is involved in an entry signal pattern, the zone would remain open. For example, #3 on this chart could have turned out to be part of a valid Fakie pattern. If it did turn out to be a valid Fakie Pattern, then the trade would be taken and the zone would be considered still open.

Also note that one can take trades anywhere within the zone. In fact, there really only needs to be on tick/pip of an entry signal touching some part of the zone for the signal to be considered. So if there are 5 candles in your entry signal pattern, only one tick or pip of one of the intervals has to be touching the zone.
